newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: SUPER SURCHARGE MAY BE CHANGED
The Federal Opposition may be able to force changes to the Government's planned superannuation surcharge now that the Coalition won't accept the vote of Independent Senator Mal Colston.
The Opposition fears the levy on high income earners could also hit low and middle income earners who don't supply their tax file numbers.
If the contentious surcharge is amended, the Government might not get all of the A$1.5 billion of revenue it hopes to raise from it.
Government sources say while the situation is now more uncertain in the Senate, there's no gaurantee Senator Colston will support the ALP.
FOUR HELPING POLICE OVER CONSTABLE'S DEATH
Four men are helping police with inquiries into the stabbing death of a police officer during a hotel brawl at Fairfield in Sydney's south west early this morning.
Police say there was a fight outside the Cambridge Hotel, and a constable, who'd gone for an after-work drink with a colleague, was stabbed in the chest.
The constable, in his mid 20s, died later in Liverpool Hospital.
The policewoman with him was also taken to hospital with facial injuries.
HANSON VOWS TO FIGHT ABORIGINES ON NATIVE TITLE
Federal Independent MP Pauline Hanson says she'll fight Aborigines every inch of the way on their native title claims.
Ms Hanson drew applause for her stance on the issue at a meeting in the Queensland town of St George last night.
She said she believed Aborigines were out to get at least 70 percent of the land mass of Australia.
She said they planned to grant self-determination and self-management and split the nation, and the rest of the population was to pay for it.
Ms Hanson said the Prime Minister, John Howard, should be taking a stronger line on the issue.
Three hundred people attended the meeting.
GOVERNMENT WILL INVESTIGATE REPORTS LABOR HELPED UNION
The Federal Government says it will investigate reports that the former Labor Government used its resources to help a union election campaign.

The Age Newspaper has reported claims by a former Transport Workers Union official, that the Victorian offices of Senator Robert Ray and then Senator Gareth Evans were used for 8-months in 1991 and 1992 to assist the union campaign.
The report claimed union officials used the offices and equipment to conduct polling, meetings and other campaign activities.
Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith says he'll ask Administrative Services Minister David Jull to investigate the matter, and if true, see if any funds can be recovered from the union.
Mr Reith says if the claims are true, and Labor failed to declare the matter to the then minister, it would expose Labor's hypocrisy in attacking Senator Mal Colston for impropriety.
MODERATE DRINKING HELPS PREVENT HEART DISEASE - STUDY
Researchers at the University of Newcastle say their finding that moderate drinking helps prevent heart attacks, should not be use to promote alcohol.

The ten-year study, published in the latest British Medical Journal, found that people who had one or two drinks a day on five or six days a week had a substantially reduced risk of a heart attack than non-drinkers.
But those who had nine or more drinks on one or two days a week were more likely to suffer a heart attack than non-drinkers.
The study was undertaken by Patrick McElduff and Annette Dobson from Newcastle University's Centre for Clinical Epidemiology and Biostatistics.
They monitored the drinking habits of nine-thousand people aged 35 to 69.
WALLIS LAKE OYSTERS CLEARED
Wallis Lake oyster farmers have been cleared to sell their product again.
A special government taskforce gave the go-ahead yesterday, following weeks of investigations into a Hepatitis A outbreak linked to the lake's oysters.
State Environemnt Minister, Pam Allan, says the taskforce's satisfied the oysters are now free from Hepatitis A.
And she says they've also implemented a range of measures to assist in protecting the lake in the future.
EUTHANASIA WATERS MUDDIED BY MP'S STANCE ON NEW DEATH
The death of a woman who entered a four-day, drug-induced coma before she died has been cited by a euthanasia opponent as proof that Australia doesn't need voluntary euthanasia laws.
Federal Liberal backbencher, Kevin Andrews, sponsored the bill which overturned the Northern Territory's voluntary euthanasia law.
Mr Andrews says the death of 56-year-old Esther Wild, who was denied the chance to die under the Territory's law, shows doctors can act ethically without resorting to lethal injections.
He says it demonstrates that Australia's laws are sufficient to deal with terminally ill people.
Ms Wild's coma was induced by drugs supplied by euthanasia advocate, Dr Philip Nitschke.
